question: What stays fixed when a theme acquires faster notes?
intro: A D♭-major theme keeps its harmonic outline while three variations divide the pulse more finely. Follow the bass beneath the decoration, then the diminished chord that prevents a self-contained ending.

sections.label: Theme · D♭ major
sections.mNote: Chordal theme in two repeated halves

sections.label: Variation 1 · displaced chords
sections.mNote: Bass and upper chords no longer strike together

sections.label: Variation 2 · semiquavers
sections.mNote: Broken chords divide the pulse more finely

sections.label: Variation 3 · demisemiquavers
sections.mNote: Faster figuration changes hands beneath and above the theme

sections.label: Theme · return
sections.mNote: Simpler theme returns without its original repeats

sections.label: Link · diminished seventh
sections.mNote: D♭-major closure is diverted towards the F-minor finale

cues.title: Chords establish the theme
cues.text: The theme moves in measured chords in D♭ major, with a gently dotted rhythm. Listen to the bass and the top of each chord together: later variations keep the harmonic route recognisable while changing how the notes are distributed.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 14, gives the Andante con moto theme in 2/4: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0 . The report’s opening has low onset density, mostly 0.4–0.6 detected attacks per second through 0:35; this is a texture indicator, not a beat count.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two repeated halves
cues.text: The theme has two halves, each repeated. Its later half reaches further harmonically and rises more strongly before returning to D♭. Keep that sequence of departure and return in mind; the variations preserve the outline beneath their changing surfaces.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 14, marks both halves for repetition. The report’s 0:46 boundary separates the quieter opening span from stronger waves around 0:55–1:00 and 1:20–1:25. The cue describes the whole theme, not a precisely timed repeat sign.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A named dedicatee
cues.text: The sonata is dedicated to Count Franz Brunsvik. Its original title page identifies the patron and the work as a sonata; the familiar “Appassionata” nickname belongs to a later publication history, not to this dedication.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus identifies the dedication and explains the later nickname in its work catalogue: https://www.beethoven.de/en/work/view/5292968940404736 .

cues.title: Chords after the bass
cues.text: In the first variation, the bass sounds before the upper chords, putting weight between the beats. The harmony remains recognisable, but the parts no longer arrive together as they did in the theme. Listen for the separation rather than for a new melody.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 14, first variation, displaces upper chords against the bass. The 1:32 novelty peak and rise in detected onset density around 1:40–1:50 support the approximate 1:34 variation boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Marie Bigot’s manuscript
cues.text: The pianist Marie Bigot owned Beethoven’s autograph of this sonata. Beethoven-Haus reports that he gave it to her after it had served for engraving. The manuscript is now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France.
cues.evidence: Beethoven-Haus work catalogue, history of the autograph and Marie Bigot’s ownership: https://www.beethoven.de/en/work/view/5292968940404736 . This cue does not repeat the associated storm anecdote as established fact.

cues.title: Harmony becomes flowing notes
cues.text: The second variation unfolds the chords into connected semiquavers. The quicker surface does not erase the slower harmonic rhythm: follow the underlying arrivals rather than trying to count every note in the upper line.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 14–15, marks the semiquaver variation p sempre ligato. The report has a quiet boundary around 2:45 followed by a rise from roughly 1.8–2.6 to 3.0–4.0 detected attacks per second through the next span; 2:46 is approximate.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A pianist with singers
cues.text: Schnabel’s musical work included extensive collaboration with the singer Therese Behr, whom he married in 1905. The Schnabel Music Foundation documents their Berlin Schubert programmes in 1928 alongside his solo Beethoven cycles.
cues.evidence: Schnabel Music Foundation biography, marriage, song collaboration and Berlin programmes: https://schnabelmusicfoundation.org/musicians/artur-schnabel/ . No causal claim about this performance’s phrasing is inferred from the biography.

cues.title: The surface divides again
cues.text: The third variation uses demisemiquavers — twice the written subdivision of the preceding variation. The rapid figures change hands while the theme takes a more sustained, sometimes syncopated form. Follow the slower notes through the moving accompaniment.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 15–16, transfers the demisemiquaver figuration between hands. The report’s onset density rises to 4.8–6.6 per second around 3:55–4:15, with a higher relative level, anchoring the approximate 3:54 start.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Across the last flourish
cues.text: Near the variation’s end, the fast notes spread through the registers and descend into a quieter space. Keep the theme’s chordal pace in mind: the simpler return will recover that scale of movement without repeating the entire opening layout.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 16, places a fortissimo descending run and diminuendo before the theme’s return. The report peaks in onset density around 4:45, then drops sharply at 4:50–4:55. This is a surrounding-passage description.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The theme without repeats
cues.text: The theme returns in simpler clothing, without the two repeated halves that made its first appearance expansive. Its measured chordal rhythm is recognisable after the faster variations, but this compressed return is heading towards a different final chord.
cues.evidence: First edition, p. 16, restores the theme without repeat signs before the final link. The report’s low level and reduced onset density from 4:55 through 5:30 support the returning-theme span beginning approximately at 4:54.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A chord looking forward
cues.text: The expected D♭-major ending is displaced by a diminished seventh, E–G–B♭–D♭. Beethoven holds and repeats the chord, then writes attacca: continue directly. The finale takes over this unstable harmony instead of beginning after a settled slow-movement conclusion.
cues.evidence: First edition, pp. 16–17, shows the diminished-seventh chords under fermatas and attacca into the finale. The report’s strongest changes at 5:42 and 5:46 locate the final harmonic disruption; the separate digital file lasts 360.1 seconds, so no gapless digital playback is asserted.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bass and chords separate
transitions.how: The theme’s repeated second half closes in D♭ major. The first variation retains that tonal framework but separates the bass from the upper chords: their displaced attacks animate the same harmonic sequence. Beethoven changes the placement of notes within the pulse rather than introducing a contrasting key or a new tune. The theme’s chordal identity remains audible through the syncopation.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 14, supplies the cadence and first variation: https://www.beethoven.de/en/media/view/6661552451092480?page=0 . The 1:32 novelty peak, quiet 1:35 window and subsequent increase in detected attacks support the approximate 1:34 join.

transitions.title: Displaced chords unfold into semiquavers
transitions.how: After the first variation’s D♭-major close, the same harmonic route begins again with connected semiquaver figures. The bass retains the slower framework while the upper notes spell out the chords in succession. Beethoven writes sempre ligato: the change is from separated chordal attacks to a flowing line, not a change of metre. The increase in subdivision gives motion without abandoning the theme.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 14–15, supplies the second variation and sempre ligato instruction. Relative level falls around 2:40–2:45, then onset density rises to roughly 3–4 detected attacks per second. The 2:46 boundary is estimated from this change and score order.

transitions.title: The subdivision doubles once more
transitions.how: The second variation reaches its cadence, but the next variation immediately refills the texture with demisemiquavers. The quicker figuration first supports the theme from below and later moves above it, so changing register and hand assignment become part of the variation. The D♭-major harmonic scheme remains the reference point while sustained and syncopated notes carry the melody against the faster stream.
transitions.evidence: First edition, pp. 15–16, gives the demisemiquaver variation and exchanges between hands. The report rises from approximately 3.8–4.0 detected attacks per second around 3:45–3:50 to 4.8–6.6 around 3:55–4:15; 3:54 is a passage estimate.

transitions.title: The descending run yields to chords
transitions.how: The third variation’s high-register growth ends in a descending run and diminuendo. The theme’s slower chordal rhythm then returns in D♭ major, with the original repeats omitted. Beethoven reduces both the density of attacks and the amount of repetition: the return recovers the theme’s identity without recreating its full opening duration.
transitions.evidence: First edition, p. 16, shows the run, diminuendo and unrepeated returning theme. The report drops from 7.8 detected attacks per second at 4:45 to 0.8 at 4:55, with a substantial fall in relative level. The 4:54 join is approximate.

transitions.title: Diminished harmony prevents a settled ending
transitions.how: Instead of leaving the theme on a final D♭-major tonic, Beethoven turns to E–G–B♭–D♭, a diminished seventh pointing towards F minor. D♭ survives as a common note while the other pitches change its harmonic setting. Fermatas suspend the rolled chords, first very quiet and then forceful. The instruction attacca carries this unresolved harmony into the finale, which begins by repeating the chord.
transitions.evidence: First edition, end of p. 16 and opening of p. 17, supplies the pitches, dynamics, fermatas and attacca. The report’s strongest novelty peaks at 5:42 and 5:46 anchor this final link. The musical attacca is distinguished from the spacing of the separate MP3 files.

fields.note: Archive description, embedded artist tag and discography agree. Bloesch identifies a Bechstein piano in Studio No. 3 for the session; no instrument serial number is established.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The original solo-piano movement is identified, but Schnabel’s performing edition and editorial alterations are not documented. The listening commentary uses the viewable original edition, plate 521; that does not establish the score used in 1933. The musical attacca into movement III is distinguished from the spacing of the separately hosted MP3 files.

fields.note: The original complete-sonata issue was HMV DB 2215–2217 in Beethoven Sonata Society Volume 5, within set DB 2211–2217. The selected digital file does not identify the pressing or reissue from which it was made; its source-carrier catalogue number remains unknown.

fields.note: No engineer is credited for the selected MP3. The uploader recordplayer78 is not identified as the transfer engineer or rights owner. fields.note: Beethoven died in 1827. The historical score is distinct from any unidentified modern performing edition. The composition’s term does not establish the rights in Schnabel’s recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: original sound recording first published in 1934.
fields.note: The Public Domain Project release-set catalogue explicitly dates first release of HMV DB 2211–2217 to 1934. Bloesch identifies the Appassionata issue as DB 2215–2217, matrices 2B 6605–6610, establishing publication separately from the 11 April 1933 recording date. Under the programme’s territorial EU rule, the earlier 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established; no worldwide clearance is claimed. Archive’s Public Domain Mark is not an ownership release, and the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not relied upon. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

composer.epithet: A pianist who turned small rhythmic cells into long arguments, then rebuilt the forms that contained them.
facts: Christian Gottlob Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Johann Georg Albrechtsberger and Antonio Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792 · Vienna and its surrounding villages thereafter
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · one opera
Progressive hearing loss documented in letters from 1801; conversation books used from 1818
composer.background:
Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770, probably on 16 December, and baptised on 17 December. His father Johann sang in the electoral court chapel, and his grandfather Ludwig had been its Kapellmeister. The family name came from the Low Countries; the ‘van’ did not indicate nobility. Johann attempted to present his son as a child prodigy, but Beethoven’s more substantial training came from Christian Gottlob Neefe, who introduced him to Bach’s keyboard music and helped him obtain work as an organist. Playing viola in the court orchestra also gave him practical knowledge of instrumental and operatic repertory.

The Bonn years supplied more than a musical apprenticeship. The court of Elector Maximilian Franz, educated patrons and friends such as the Breuning family brought Beethoven into contact with Enlightenment literature and social ideas. After his mother’s death in 1787 and his father’s worsening incapacity, he assumed increasing responsibility for the household. In 1792 he left for Vienna to study with Haydn. The intended period of further training became permanent residence: the French occupation of Bonn in 1794 ended the old electoral establishment to which he might have returned.
